profile.documented: A chat model documented for text, tools, and vision use with no thinking mode, a claimed 262144-token working context, and broad multilingual coverage that is not enumerated per language. Sampling follows plain greedy harness defaults, no packaged stop sequences are declared, and tool use is marked as documented from runtime capabilities. profile.role_in_run: No HOME test was designed around this model, so it ran the whole program as a guest. Its 351 records span 22 scored tests, though 96 cases across thirteen tests never ran for budget reasons and dilute its coverage.

overall.rating_basis: Rating 6.4 = 10 * (0.7 * 0.785 mean quality over 22 scored tests + 0.3 * 0.298 OK rate over 245 scored records); no home-test term exists because the model has no home test, so the freed weight sits on mean quality.

failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: All 108 cases carry valid JSON with the right fields and values inside triple-backtick fences; the validator keeps the semantic score, for example 0.941 on the classification test, and zeroes only the strict score.
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Every fenced answer fails strict validation, so the model is unusable in pipelines that parse output directly, however correct the content.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: a format defect recorded without a machine-readable sub-reason
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: Thirty-four of the 35 are fenced JSON payloads like the code-fence pattern above; the remaining one is free prose answering a vision tool call instead of emitting the call.
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: The practical effect matches the fence pattern: content the validator scores highly cannot be consumed without a postprocessing step.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: the final answer broke the output contract with extra text or fenced JSON
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: Nine of the ten answers score a full 1.000 semantic quality with one at 0.5, but all ten present fenced JSON or surrounding prose where the contract demands a bare answer.
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Contract breaks are the cheapest failures to fix from outside: a fence-stripping parser recovers all of this quality with no model change.

strengths: Its semantic content is outstanding: mean quality 0.785 over 22 scored tests, with seven tests at a perfect 1.000 including safety, RAG, wiki questions, and template extraction.
Its code repair is solid at 0.917, with ten of twelve patches clean against hidden tests.
Its OCR transcription reached 0.981 over ten scored images, the best transcription figure among the guest models.
It attempted every vision tool-calling case and scored 0.700, showing its documented vision capability is operational rather than nominal.
weaknesses: It wraps essentially every structured answer in code fences the contracts forbid: 108 fence defects plus 34 more fenced payloads logged without a detailed sub-reason, driving strict quality to zero on eleven tests.
It failed visual grounding at 0.083, with essentially no correct bounding box across twelve cases.
Chart reading is weak at 0.417, so its vision capability covers documents and OCR far better than charts and coordinates.
Ninety-six cases across thirteen tests never ran for budget reasons, so its strong means rest on thinner evidence than the runner planned.
use_when: Bug repair and code review workflows where a human or a fence-stripping postprocessor reads the patch, since the code inside the fences is usually right.
Safety classification and RAG answering behind a lenient parser that strips markdown fences before validation.
OCR transcription of mixed-language images where plain-text answers are accepted.
Document understanding tasks where answer content matters more than the exact output envelope.
avoid_when: Strict machine-readable pipelines that reject fenced JSON, where every answer would fail validation despite correct content.
Visual grounding that needs accurate bounding-box coordinates, where it scored near zero.
Chart-value extraction presented as exact numbers, where fewer than half its answers were right.
hardware_fit: Cold load takes about 52 seconds, the cost of bringing roughly 6 GB onto the card, and the first token needs a further 44 seconds, so interactive restarts feel slow. Steady generation near 57 tok/s is respectable once it starts, and no partial-offload slowdown is recorded for this run. The practical consequence is batch-friendly but restart-hostile behavior: keep it loaded and it serves well, reload it often and the clock dominates.
bottom_line: A model that knows the answers but cannot package them: top-tier semantic content dragged to a 6.4 rating by a universal code-fence habit that zeroes strict quality test after test. Put a fence-stripping parser in front of it and it is excellent; validate strictly and it scores nothing.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: the correct document was not ranked first
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: As an embedding model it emits no text at all, so there is no sentence to quote; the failure is purely ordinal, with the reference document landing lower in the similarity ranking at partial credit.
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Misranked queries need a reranking stage or a larger candidate list, since the signal is present but not top-1.

strengths: It is a capable English retriever at 0.902, with 20 of 30 queries fully correct.
Its cross-lingual retrieval at 0.781 across all 40 queries shows usable transfer beyond English, with 21 fully correct rankings.
Its 3584-dimensional vectors give downstream rerankers a rich representation, verified live at import time.
It completed both eligible tests in full with zero unrun cases, so its two means are the best-evidenced in this group per test.
weaknesses: It is a single-capability model: 22 of 24 tests hold placeholders only, so nothing can be said about generation, reasoning, tools, or vision.
Nineteen of forty cross-lingual rankings are only partial, so top-1 precision drops when queries leave English.
Ten of thirty English rankings are partial as well, meaning roughly a third of queries would need a reranking stage.
Its 7.6 rating rests on just two retrieval tests and must not be compared with generalist ratings earned across seventeen or more tests.
use_when: English document and code retrieval as a first-stage candidate generator feeding a reranker.
Cross-lingual retrieval shortlists where approximate ranking is acceptable and a later stage picks the winner.
Embedding sidecar duty next to a generative model, supplying vectors while the other model writes answers.
avoid_when: Any task that needs text out: classification labels, answers, code, or tool calls are all outside its single capability.
Top-1-critical retrieval without a reranker, where its partial rankings would surface the wrong document.
Vision or audio workloads, which need capabilities this profile does not document.
hardware_fit: Cold load takes about 64 seconds for its 4.38 GB, the smallest footprint of the four, and as an embedding-only model it has no generation speed or first-token latency to report. Throughput is measured in queries rather than tokens, and both retrieval tests completed in full. The practical consequence is a cheap retrieval sidecar: slow to first readiness, then quiet and compact next to a generative model.
bottom_line: A retrieval specialist that does exactly one job well: 0.902 English and 0.781 cross-lingual retrieval with fully completed tests. Its 7.6 rating describes two retrieval tests only and must never be read as a generalist score.

bottom_line: The highest-rated model in this group at 7.9 and the cleanest formatter, with genuinely exercised vision capability across charts, documents, grounding, OCR, and tool calls. Grounding coordinates and optimization constraints are its blind spots, and budget left 142 of its cases unrun.

failure_analysis.example_quote:
# New Engineer Onboarding

This guide explains `make setup` with a **first Friday demo** setup and an *open questions*. See the [handbook](https://docs.example.com/hr/handbook) for background.

## Wee[truncated]
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Near-miss conversions pass human review but fail exact validators, so pipelines must decide whether detail-level fidelity matters.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: the request was routed to the wrong queue
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: Five support requests got a valid-looking route object pointing at the wrong team, for example a TECH route with a technical keyword where policy demanded otherwise.
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: A confident wrong route sends the customer to the wrong team, which is worse operationally than an abstention.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: the final answer was cut short by the token limit
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: Four answers exceed 600 characters of correct content and stop mid-structure with a length stop, two on the log-tracking test and one each on safety and function calling.
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Truncated structured answers are unparseable, so the correct prefix is wasted whenever the budget clips the closing brackets.

failure_analysis.english_meaning: the tool calls were right but a duplicated side effect corrupted the end state
failure_analysis.what_the_model_did: On three loop cases the model performed the correct action and then performed it again, for example sending the same refund email twice, which the state check rejects.
failure_analysis.why_it_matters: Duplicate tool calls turn correct behavior into real-world harm whenever the action is not idempotent, as with sent emails.

strengths: It earned the highest clean-answer rate of the four at 80.7 percent over 274 scored records, combining strong language transfer with disciplined output contracts.
It solved every case on three whole tests: long-context wiki questions, multi-step word problems, and single-turn function calls, all at 1.000.
Its tool behavior is reliable in the common case, with 29 of 30 single-turn calls and 13 of 16 code generations fully correct.
It kept strict-format quality equal to semantic quality on most tests, so its answers can be parsed as well as read, unlike the fence-prone models in this group.
weaknesses: Its thinking mode is a liability under fixed token budgets: 24 reasoning-trace overflows produced no answer at all on math, code repair, and optimization tasks.
It failed multilingual log state tracking completely at 0.000, with both attempted cases cut off mid-answer and the third exceeding the context window.
It misrouted five of forty support requests and lost two more to timeouts, so policy routing degrades at volume.
use_when: Multilingual support-message classification where strict JSON output is parsed by downstream code.
Long-context wiki question answering and multi-step word problems with generous per-case token budgets.
Single-turn function calling and short tool loops where each call is validated before execution.
Grounded RAG answering with citations over provided passages.
avoid_when: Competition math and constrained optimization with thinking enabled under tight token budgets, where reasoning overflows erase the whole answer.
Multilingual log state tracking over long evidence lists, where its answers were cut off before completion.
Tool loops where a duplicated side effect is expensive: it sent the same refund email twice on one loop case.
hardware_fit: Cold load takes about 3 seconds with the full 5.33 GB resident on the GPU at offload ratio 1.00, so restarts are nearly free on this 8 GB card. Steady generation runs near 67 tok/s, the fastest of the four, while the 36.5-second first-token latency reflects thinking mode rather than slow hardware. The practical result is a model that starts instantly and streams quickly once its reasoning trace resolves.
bottom_line: The strongest generalist guest in this group: broadest coverage at 17 scored tests, highest clean-answer rate at 80 percent, and strict-parseable output almost everywhere. Its thinking mode is the one real caveat, erasing answers on math-style tasks whenever the token budget runs out first.
